newsitem.title: USA: U.S. evacuates nearly 1,000 people from Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. evacuates nearly 1,000 people from Sierra Leone.

text.p: U.S. military helicopters safely evacuated more than 900 Americans, foreigners and some deposed government officials from Sierra Leone on Friday and the U.S. embassy was ordered closed, officials said.

They said about 330 Americans and 600 people from 40 other countries were taken by helicopter from Freetown to the helicopter carrier USS Kearsarge following Sunday's military coup against the civilian rulers of the West African nation.
They said several officials of the toppled government, including a deputy defence minister, the minister of planning, and some civic group leaders, were included in the evacuation.

State Department spokesman John Dinger said the evacuation and embassy closure were ordered because the situation was "so potentially volatile," with competing Sierra Leone military forces as well as Nigerian troops on the ground.

Naval Capt. Greg Ertel, who spoke to reporters at the Pentagon by satellite from the Kearsarge, said there were no injuries and neither the helicopters nor the 200 troops on the ground were fired on during the evacuation.

The evacuees included about 200 children and a woman who was in labour said Ertel, the commander of an amphibious unit which includes the Kearsarge. He said the ship, though crowded, was stocked with ice cream, brownies and cookies.

U.S. Charge d'affaires Ann Wright, the top U.S. diplomat there at the time of the coup, said she had offered to remain in Sierra Leone despite looting in the city and "heavy, heavy movement of troops."
But she said the State Department deemed it too big a risk and ordered the "temporary suspending" of the Embassy, which was badly damaged in nearby fighting on Sunday.
Among the security factors she cited were military fortifications near the Embassy and "what appeared to be a Nigerian military operation to restore the former (civilian) government," Wright said.
"I personally always hate to see the United States flag taken down for any reason. I was willing to stay," she said.
The State Department said local security employees were left in place at the embassy. They could neither confirm nor deny reports that the embassy was looted after the last Americans left.

Asked in Washington about the reports of a Nigerian plan to oust the coup leaders once the U.S. evacuation was over, State Department spokesman John Dinger said: "We believe there has been more than enough violence in Sierra Leone.
"We want to see democracy restored .... through diplomatic means and international pressure," Dinger said.

Marine Col. Samuel Helland, who commanded the task force and spoke on the satellite hookup, said the evacuation would be officially declared over when the last of the Marines, still en route, reach the ship.
CH-53 "Sea Stallion" helicopters, which can carry up to 55 passengers, and CH-46 "Sea Knight" helicopters, capable of taking 24, were used for the operation.
Officials said the evacuated Americans on the Kearsarge would be flown to Conakry, Guinea, about 100 miles (160 km) north of Freetown enroute to Brussels.
U.S. Ambassador John Hirsch, who was out of Sierra Leone at the time of the coup, will monitor the situation from Conakry.
